Generating continuous-time, continuous-space stochastic processes, such as videos or weather forecasts, conditioned on partial observations is a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches, like diffusion models, struggle with this task due to their reliance on Markovian assumptions, which limit their ability to model dependencies across time and space.

This work introduces a novel framework that employs non-Markovian diffusion bridges to effectively model these processes. The proposed method allows for autoregressive generation of any subset of observations, significantly improving the flexibility and performance in generating complex stochastic processes. The practical implication is enhanced capabilities in generating realistic and coherent sequences from partial data.

title: Stefano Ermon (@StefanoErmon)
summary:
The Diffusion LLM Hitting 1,000+ Tokens Per Second
Inception Labs just launched Mercury 2, and it is changing how language models generate text. Instead of outputting one word at a time sequentially, Mercury 2 is a "Diffusion LLM."
It starts with noise and refines the entire output in parallel, allowing it to blast out over 1,000 tokens per second!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HB9d2-_bgAAz1eT.jpg
Quoting @ArtificialAnlys
Inception Labs has launched Mercury 2, their next generation production-ready Diffusion LLM. Mercury 2 achieves >1,000 output tokens/s with significant gains in intelligence
@_inception_ai's Diffusion LLMs (“dLLMs”) use a different architecture compared to autoregressive based LLMs. The Diffusion LLM generation process starts with noise and iteratively refines the output using a transformer model that can modify multiple tokens in parallel. This allows parallelization of output token generation, allowing faster output speeds because many output tokens are generated at the same time.
Key takeaways:
➤ Amongst comparable size/price-class models, Mercury 2 performs competitively in intelligence vs. output speed. While it does not have leading intelligence, it’s output speed is more than 3X the next fastest model in this class (benchmarks based on first party endpoints or the median of providers serving the model where a first party endpoint is not available)
➤ Key strengths include agentic coding & terminal use and instruction following. Mercury 2 performs at similar level to Claude 4.5 Haiku on Terminal-Bench Hard and scores 70% on IFBench (Instruction Following), outperforming gpt-oss-120B, GPT-5.1 Codex mini, and GPT-5 nano
Inception Labs background:
This is the second release from Inception Labs. The founders were previously professors from Stanford, UCLA, and Cornell and have contributed to AI research & technologies including Flash Attention, Decision Transformers, and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).

title: Stefano Ermon (@StefanoErmon)
summary:
[1/D]
🤔 What are drifting models really connected to?
📢 Our new paper, A Unified View of Drifting and Score-Based Models, shows that the bridge to score-based models is clear and precise (w/ team and @mittu1204, @StefanoErmon, @MoleiTaoMath)!
✍️ Main takeaway: drifting is more closely connected to score-based (diffusion) modeling than it may first appear!
🔗
🎯 Here’s why:
Drifting’s mean-shift moves a sample toward the kernel-weighted average of nearby samples.
Score function points toward regions of higher density.
So both describe local directions that push samples toward where data is denser.
We show that this link is exact for Gaussian kernels (Section 4.1):
📌drifting’s mean-shift = a rescaled score-matching field between the Gaussian-smoothed data and model distributions — the vector field underlying score matching (Tweedie!).
📌This also clarifies the bridge to Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD): both use score-based transport directions, but only differ in how the score is realized—drifting does so nonparametrically through kernel neighborhoods, whereas DMD relies on a pretrained diffusion teacher.
🤔 So what happens for the default Laplace kernel used in drifting models? Let’s look below 👇

title: Stefano Ermon (@StefanoErmon)
summary:
We reasoning-architected Mercury-2: 80% accuracy at 503ms TTFB. Two-phase variant: 62% accuracy, 376ms latency.
The only variable: whether domain reasoning is pre-structured before generation begins. Raw Mercury-2 scores 10%. Architected scores 80%. +70pp from architecture alone.
On the emotional intelligence test (10 episodes), both raw models score 0% regardless of model size. The failure is not lack of emotional awareness. Both open with empathetic language. The failure compounds: they pivot to health content on life moments (substantive failure) and produce 30+ sentence responses where 2 to 3 are appropriate (structural failure). The raw system prompt ("You are a health coach. Answer the patient.") provides no instruction to withhold advice. The 0% EQ reflects the absence of constraint architecture.
A patient says "my dad passed away last week." The raw model pivots to dry health content and actionable suggestions. In healthcare coaching, that is a clinical misstep, not a communication style. The correct response is acknowledgment as is taught.
The architected version produces: "I can only imagine how hard this must be. I'm here if you want to talk." It scores 90% on the same EQ test. This is emergent: the architecture detects the emotional signal through a single focus directive and sequences the concerns across turns.
Empathy first communication, health coaching when the patient signals readiness. While it does not drop health coaching role.

Check out our CVPR 2026 paper. Spectrum accelerates diffusion sampling by estimating features using Chebychev polynomials instead of costly network evaluations. This approach achieves significant speedups while maintaining image and video quality.

Diffusion models produce impressive images and videos, but sampling is slow because each output requires many expensive forward passes through the model. Spectrum proposes skipping most of these passes by predicting features adaptively in the spectral domain, enabling faster sampling without sacrificing quality. The work is part of a collaboration with Juntong Shi, Puheng Li, Haotian Ye, Qiushan Guo, and Stefano Ermon, and the project includes community-contributed tools for diffusion models. LLM-assisted search in verifiable domains is incredibly exciting right now. The model matters, but so does the algorithmic harness used to explore the search space and iterate toward better solutions.
We’re excited to describe a new search algorithm that makes this exploration process more effective, leading to the results below with open-source models:
✨ Mathematics: new state-of-the-art constructions for the Erdős Minimum Overlap Problem
⚛️Quantum computing: improved quantum circuit compilation, reducing SWAP overhead by 24.5% on IBM Q20.
⚡️ AI infrastructure: designed a highly efficient TriMul Triton kernel, improving on prior human- and AI-designed implementations.
More details in the blog:
Great collaboration by WILL, @Stanford, @PKU1898, @Tsinghua_Uni, and @HKUSTGuangzhou.

summary:
RamaX screens large naive or AI-designed libraries at incredible speed (<1 week). But how accurate is it?
Answer ➡️very
Our new case study shows RamaX has high precision and recall on a benchmark minibinder set. We also share two partner projects where we go from AI design to data in <2 weeks—and find binders that computational metrics miss. Library-scale screening is critical.

✨ A new “Road Ahead” chapter on discrete diffusion
